title: Goecha La and Dzongri trek: permits, cost, season
meta_description: Goecha La and Dzongri treks from Yuksom: permits, KNP fees, 2026 costs, best months, grading, day-by-day altitudes and park rules, from a Gangtok-based team.
summary: Goecha La is a 9–10 day round trek from Yuksom (1,780 m) through Khangchendzonga National Park to a viewpoint at about 4,570 m below Kangchenjunga; Dzongri (4,020 m) is the 5–6 day short version. Both need park permits and a registered guide. Expect ₹22,000–30,000 for a group departure and more for a private team.

sections.heading: Two treks on one trail
paras: Both treks start at Yuksom, the old capital of the Namgyal kings in Gyalshing district (West Sikkim), and follow the same path up the Prek Chu valley into Khangchendzonga National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016. The trail climbs through subtropical forest, then oak, magnolia and rhododendron, to the meadows of Dzongri at about 4,020 m. From there the short trek turns back, and the long trek continues to Thansing, Lamuney and the Goecha La viewpoint facing the south-east face of Kangchenjunga (8,586 m).

The Sikkim Forest Department describes the Goecha La–Dzongri route as 45 km long and gives 4,570 m for Goecha La in its 2025 press note on the trail. Wikipedia lists the actual pass at 4,940 m, which trekkers do not reach: groups normally stop at the first viewpoint below it. The higher viewpoints have been closed to protect the alpine habitat. Rules like this change, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The Dzongri short trek
paras: If you have a week rather than eleven days, Dzongri gives you most of the mountain for half the effort. The plan is Yuksom to Sachen, Sachen to Tshoka, Tshoka to Dzongri, then a pre-dawn climb to Dzongri Top for sunrise on Kabru, Rathong, Kangchenjunga and Pandim, and the walk down to Tshoka the same day. A last day takes you back to Yuksom. With the drives from NJP, that is six nights.

Dzongri is open meadow above the tree line, with prayer flags, stone shelters and a basic trekkers' hut, and it feels very different from the forest below. Weather on the top changes within minutes, so leave the camp by 4 am in October and be patient: cloud often lifts briefly after sunrise.

sections.heading: Permits and park rules
paras: Indian citizens do not need an inner line permit for Sikkim, but every trekker needs a Khangchendzonga National Park entry permit and must register at Yuksom before starting. The park fee has been about ₹350 per Indian for the first seven days and ₹40 for each extra day, and about ₹560 per foreign national for seven days plus ₹80 a day after that, with separate camping, guide and porter charges. Your registered trekking agent arranges the paperwork at Yuksom with photo ID; carry two photocopies and passport photos.

Foreign nationals first need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, applied for online on the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India, and then a Protected Area Permit for Dzongri and Goecha La, issued only to groups of two or more through a registered agent. Solo trekking is not allowed for anyone: a registered local guide is mandatory. These are the rules as we understand them; check current status before you travel.
list: No camping at Samiti Lake: it is sacred to both Bhutia and Lepcha communities, and the Forest Department forbids it.
Carry out every wrapper, battery and bottle; the park checks bags for plastic at Yuksom.
No wood fires: cooking is on kerosene or gas carried by your team.
Stay on the marked trail and inside the permitted area; the pass itself is off-limits.

sections.heading: What it costs in 2026
paras: Fixed group departures from Yuksom, with tents, a cook, a guide, food and park fees, cost roughly ₹22,000–30,000 per person plus 5 per cent GST for the full Goecha La trek, and roughly ₹13,000–18,000 for Dzongri. Shared transport from NJP to Yuksom and back usually costs another ₹2,000–3,500 per person. A private trek with your own guide, cook and porters is far more flexible and costs roughly ₹45,000–70,000 per person for two people, falling as the group grows.

Extra costs to plan for: offloading your rucksack onto a porter or pack animal, usually ₹400–600 per day per bag; a night in Yuksom before and after the trek; tips for the guide, cook and porters; and rental gear if you lack a warm sleeping bag or down jacket. All figures are indicative.

sections.heading: Choosing a trekking team
paras: Pick a team registered with Sikkim Tourism or the Travel Agents Association of Sikkim, because only registered agents can process park permits. Ask how many trekkers share a guide (one guide for up to eight is reasonable), whether the guide holds first-aid training, what oxygen and medical kit the team carries, and what happens if you need to turn back. A good team will tell you plainly that the summit-day start depends on weather and your health, not on the schedule.

Ask also about the kitchen: how water is treated, what food comes on the trail and how waste is carried out. On our own treks the team carries all rubbish back to Yuksom, and we hire guides, cooks and porters from Yuksom and nearby villages, so the money stays in the valley the trail passes through.

sections.heading: Best season and grading
paras: There are two seasons. April to mid-May brings rhododendrons in flower between Bakhim and Phedang, with warmer nights but more afternoon cloud. Late September to November brings the clearest mountain views, cold nights (well below freezing at Lamuney) and crisp mornings. December can be clear but very cold, with snow on the upper trail, and many teams stop running by mid-December. We do not run treks in the June–August monsoon, when leeches, slips and cloud take over the lower trail.

We grade Goecha La as moderate to difficult. Daily climbs of 700–1,000 m, two long days of 15 km and the summit-day start at about 3 am need real fitness: aim to jog 5 km in 35 minutes or walk 10 km with a light pack before you come. Dzongri is moderate: shorter, but it still takes you above 4,000 m in four days.

sections.heading: Altitude, health and what to pack
paras: The trail gains about 2,200 m in the three days from Yuksom to Dzongri, which is why the rest day at Dzongri matters. Headache, nausea, loss of appetite and unusual breathlessness at rest are signs of acute mountain sickness. Tell your guide at once. The cure for anything worse than a mild headache is to descend, and good teams carry oxygen and a pulse oximeter.

Drink 3–4 litres of water a day, eat even when you are not hungry, avoid alcohol on the trail and do not race ahead of the group. Talk to your doctor before the trip if you have heart, lung or blood pressure conditions, and ask about acetazolamide.
Layering beats bulk. Mornings at Dzongri in October are often around -5 °C, while the afternoon walk below Tshoka can be warm and humid.
list: Broken-in trekking shoes with ankle support, plus camp sandals
Down jacket, fleece, thermal base layers, rain jacket and rain pants
Warm hat, sun cap, gloves (inner and outer), woollen socks
Sunglasses rated UV400, sunscreen and lip balm
Two 1-litre bottles or a hydration bladder, and a refillable bottle for Yuksom
Headlamp with spare batteries for the summit-day start
Personal medicines, a small first-aid kit and photo ID copies

faqs.q: How many days does the Goecha La trek take?
faqs.a: The classic route takes 9 walking days from Yuksom and back, so most trips are 11 days from NJP including the drives. That includes a rest and acclimatisation day at Dzongri. A shorter plan that skips the rest day is possible but raises the risk of altitude sickness. Dzongri alone takes 5–6 days from Yuksom.

faqs.q: How much does the Goecha La trek cost?
faqs.a: Group departures from Yuksom cost roughly ₹22,000–30,000 per person plus GST, including tents, food, guide, cook and park fees. Add ₹2,000–3,500 for shared transport from NJP, plus offloading at ₹400–600 a day if you want a porter to carry your rucksack. A private trek for two costs about ₹45,000–70,000 per person. Figures are indicative for 2026.

faqs.q: Can foreigners do the Goecha La trek?
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, applied for online on the e-FRRO portal, and a Protected Area Permit for Dzongri and Goecha La. The PAP is issued only to groups of two or more through a registered agent, and a licensed guide must accompany the group. Check current status before you travel, as permit rules change.

faqs.q: Can I trek to Goecha La without a guide?
faqs.a: No. Solo and unguided trekking is not allowed in Khangchendzonga National Park. Every group must register at Yuksom with a registered local guide, and the park checks permits along the trail. A guide also matters for safety: weather above Dzongri changes fast and the summit-day start is in the dark.

faqs.q: What is the best month for Goecha La?
faqs.a: October and early November give the clearest views of Kangchenjunga and the most stable weather, with very cold nights. April to mid-May is the rhododendron season, with milder nights and more afternoon cloud. Avoid June to August, when monsoon rain, leeches and cloud make the trail slippery and the views rare.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Goecha La trek?
faqs.a: Moderate to difficult. You climb from 1,780 m to about 4,570 m, walk 5–8 hours on most days and face a 10–12 hour summit day starting around 3 am. Previous trekking experience helps but is not essential if you train for six to eight weeks and can walk 10 km with a light pack comfortably.

faqs.q: Is the Dzongri trek good for beginners?
faqs.a: It is one of the better first high-altitude treks in Sikkim, because it is short and the views from Dzongri Top over Kabru, Pandim and Kangchenjunga are close to those on the full trek. It still climbs above 4,000 m in four days, so fitness and a slow pace matter. Fit teenagers and active adults usually manage well.

faqs.q: Where do you sleep on the Goecha La trek?
faqs.a: Mostly in tents at designated campsites. Tshoka, Dzongri and Thansing also have basic trekkers' huts run by the forest department, but in season most groups camp. Your first and last nights are in Yuksom in a lodge or homestay. Samiti Lake is closed to camping because it is sacred to Bhutia and Lepcha communities.

faqs.q: Can I reach the actual Goecha La pass?
faqs.a: Normally no. Trekkers stop at the first viewpoint below the pass, at about 4,570 m by the Forest Department's figure, which faces Kangchenjunga directly. The pass itself, given as 4,940 m on Wikipedia, and the higher viewpoints have been closed to protect the alpine zone. Check current status before you travel.
